Three principle peaks corresponding to the position of Ta are located as noted for both powder and sintered samples.
Three principle peaks corresponding to the position of Ta are located as noted for both powder and sintered samples.

Clear W peaks are observed for powders in W containing samples in 5(a). These peaks are elevated in intensity in comparison to the expected intensity by atomic percent, likely as tungsten is found on top of Ta powder and is acting to block x-rays from penetrating the full Ta surface. In the sintered samples in 5(b) the tungsten peaks are found to be drastically reduced in intensity and slightly shifted to lower angles. These W peaks are found to overlap with the principle tantalum peaks.

Small peaks corresponding to Ta2C and TiC are also present in the Ta-10vol%W-1.5vol%TiC sample, suggesting some reaction of TiC with Ta possibly forming either Ta-Ti alloys or a TiOx phase within the material.

Ti rich regions are noted in the mapping, and are found to correspond with several oxygen regions, suggesting the formation of a TiOx phase.
Ta 100% (4a) was found to display an average grain size of approximately 50.1±2.5 µm.
A two-phase microstructure was observed consisting of a fully contiguous tungsten-heavy phase surrounding a soft Ta-rich phase.

The microstructure of the Ta-10vol%W alloy is similar to the Ta-10vol%W-1.5vl%TiC sample (Figure 4c). Ta islands were found to be comparable in size between the two samples, as were the size of grains within each Ta region.

Mapping further showed regions of high oxygen concentration located in areas of sample porosity. As oxidation of tantalum is known to result in the formation of pores, the existence of these regions is evidence of sample oxidation 22.
EDS mapping of the Ta-10vol%W-1.5vol%TiC sample surface revealed similar to results to those seen for the Ta-10vol%W sample, with porous regions corresponding to oxygen-rich regions.
Room temperature Ta displayed ductile failure as revealed in 12(a), with dimples clearly present on the front view fracture surface.
The 1927 °C tested sample reveals a slight increase in ductility despite brittle failure indicated by river patterns in 13(b)

conditions.test_method: Vickers hardness testing, 1 kg load, ASTM E384-11

evidence.quote: The Vickers hardness number of pure Ta was found to be approximately 103.

conditions.test_method: Vickers hardness testing, 1 kg load, ASTM E384-11

evidence.quote: Addition of 10vol%W resulted in a nearly 100% increase in hardness to a Vicker’s hardness number of 204.
Young’s modulus was found to be 178.12 GPa for the pure Ta sample, which agrees with previously reported values.
Addition of 10vol%W resulted in an increase to a modulus of 192.39 GPa.
An average peak flexural strength (taken as the UFS) of 354.83 MPa prior to contact with the testing apparatus was noted for tested samples.
Addition of 10vol%W resulted in a dramatic decrease in ductility but increase of UFS to 786.14 MPa.
The Ta-10vol%W-1.5vol%TiC sample displayed the least ductility of all samples but highest UFS of 912.27 MPa.
Alloying with tungsten results in a substantially higher modulus of 55 GPa versus 12 GPa for Ta at 1927 °C.
